scenario: An internal operations agent can read customer records and, for some staff, issue account credits. Requirements: verify who each user is, allow credits only for users whose role permits them, and keep an auditable record of who did what.
stem: Which design best meets the requirements?

options.text: Embed a single service API key in the web front end and let the agent run every tool on behalf of whoever is connected.
Authenticate users with SSO, pass their identity to the backend, check role per tool call, and audit-log calls by user.
Give each employee their own Anthropic API key and let them run the agent locally against production systems.
Authenticate users with SSO at login, then let the agent use one admin credential for all tools for the session.

rationale.correct: Identity validation (SSO), access-level verification on every privileged tool call (not just at login), and authorized-access monitoring (audit logs that record which user triggered which action) together meet all three requirements. The Anthropic key and backend credentials stay server-side.

distractors.A: A key in the front end is exposed to every browser, and no per-user authorization or attribution is possible.
distractors.C: Per-user API keys say nothing about production-system entitlements, scatter credentials, and push production access onto laptops.
distractors.D: SSO verifies who logged in, but a shared admin credential means tool calls are neither authorized nor attributable per user.

scenario: Your research feature calls the Messages API with Anthropic's server-side web search and web fetch tools enabled. On long research questions some responses come back with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` and no final answer. Your loop currently treats any stop reason other than `tool_use` as finished and shows the partial text to the user.
stem: How should the application handle `pause_turn`?

options.text: Treat it as an error and resend the original request from scratch with a higher `max_tokens` so the research can finish in one response.
Send the conversation back with the paused assistant response appended and no new user message, so the server resumes its tool loop.
Append a user message saying "Continue" after the paused response, so the model knows it should keep researching where it stopped.
Execute the pending web search in your own code and return its results as a `tool_result` block, then call the API again.

rationale.correct: With server tools, the API runs its own sampling loop on Anthropic's side; when that loop hits its iteration limit it returns `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`. The client resumes by sending the conversation back with the paused assistant content included; the trailing server-tool block tells the API to pick up where it left off. The loop also needs to stop treating every non-`tool_use` stop reason as "done".

distractors.A: The pause is not a token-limit failure, and restarting throws away the searches already performed, repeating cost and latency.
distractors.C: No extra user turn is needed; the API detects the paused server-tool use and resumes on its own. Adding a synthetic message changes the conversation for no benefit.
distractors.D: Web search is a server tool executed by Anthropic, so there is no client-side `tool_use` for your code to answer; running your own search duplicates the platform's work.

scenario: You wrote a stdio MCP server in Python. It behaves correctly when you exercise it with a test harness, but when Claude Code launches it, the connection fails intermittently with JSON parse errors. You recently added `print()` statements to trace each incoming request and enabled a library that logs warnings at startup.
stem: What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

options.text: The `print()` calls write to stdout, the JSON-RPC channel under stdio; send diagnostics to stderr or a log file instead.
The server starts too slowly; raise the client's connection timeout so the initialization handshake has time to complete.
stdio can't carry structured data reliably, so switch the server's tools to resources that the client reads as files.
The tool input schemas are malformed; add `additionalProperties: false` to each schema so the client can parse the messages.

rationale.correct: With the stdio transport the client and server exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over stdin/stdout. Anything else written to stdout (debug prints, library warnings) gets interleaved with protocol messages and the client fails to parse them. Logging to stderr (which hosts typically capture) or to a file keeps the channel clean; it also explains why the server works when tested on its own.

distractors.B: A slow start would produce timeouts, not JSON parse errors, and the errors started right after stdout output was added.
distractors.C: stdio is a supported, widely used transport for local servers; the problem is extra bytes on the channel, not the transport.
distractors.D: Schema strictness controls what arguments Claude may send; it doesn't affect whether the client can parse the protocol stream.

scenario: A support org wants Claude to triage new Jira tickets: read the ticket and its linked tickets from Jira, then apply the org's 40-line triage rubric (severity definitions, routing rules, required labels) consistently. The rubric changes monthly and is owned by the support-ops team. Jira access must use each agent user's own OAuth grant.
stem: Which combination best fits these requirements?

options.text: An MCP server for Jira with per-user OAuth, plus a Skill holding the triage rubric that support-ops maintains.
A single Skill containing the rubric, a shared Jira API token, and a bundled script that calls the Jira REST API directly.
An MCP server for Jira whose tool descriptions embed the full rubric, so the routing rules ship with each Jira tool.
Custom Jira tools reimplemented inside each support app, plus the rubric pasted into each app's system prompt.

rationale.correct: The two needs are different kinds of customization. Live, per-user-authenticated access to Jira is an integration problem, which an MCP server solves once for every client. The rubric is procedural knowledge that changes monthly and has its own owner, which a Skill packages so support-ops can update it without touching the integration.

distractors.B: One shared token defeats per-user OAuth and access auditing, and coupling credentials to the rubric means routine rubric edits touch secrets.
distractors.C: Tool descriptions should say what a tool does and when to use it; stuffing a monthly-changing rubric into them bloats every listing and ties rubric changes to server releases.
distractors.D: Duplicated integrations and prompts drift across apps, and each rubric change needs edits and redeploys in every app.

scenario: A team added a community filesystem MCP server to Claude Code so Claude could "read and write files better." Sessions now show two overlapping sets of file tools, Claude alternates between them, and edits made through the MCP tools aren't covered by the path-based deny rules the team wrote for the built-in Edit and Write tools.
stem: What is the best change?

options.text: Remove the redundant filesystem MCP server and use Claude Code's built-in file tools, which honor the team's permission rules.
Keep both tool sets and add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude which of the two file toolsets to use for each kind of file.
Disable the built-in file tools so only the MCP versions remain, then write equivalent permission rules for the MCP tools later.
Wrap the filesystem MCP server in a Skill so that its tools are loaded only when Claude detects a file-related task.

rationale.correct: Built-in tools should be the default when they already cover a capability. Claude Code's Read, Edit, and Write are integrated with its permission system, so the team's deny rules apply to them. A second, overlapping set of file tools adds selection ambiguity and a path around those rules, with no capability gained.

distractors.B: A routing instruction is soft guidance; Claude may still pick either set, and the MCP tools stay outside the rules written for Edit and Write.
distractors.C: This throws away well-integrated built-ins and leaves the repository unprotected until replacement rules exist, to keep a tool that adds nothing.
distractors.D: Skills package instructions and files; they don't gate when an MCP server's tools are available, so the overlap and the permission gap remain.
